captions.instagram:
How does a tabla work?

Most drums just go thud. The tabla sings a note you can tune to a song, thanks to a black spot of iron-filing paste that C. V. Raman explained in 1920. Play the dayan and bayan in 3D, watch the drumhead's modes line up, and bend the bass with your palm.

→ A tabla is two drums: a wooden dayan for the right hand and a metal bayan for the left.
→ Each head is goatskin in layers: a rim called the kinar, open skin, and a black syahi in the middle.
→ A plain drumhead rings in patterns called modes, with still lines called nodes.
→ C. V. Raman showed why the dayan sings: its black syahi adds weight to the middle.
→ The weight pulls the overtones into line at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: a real musical note.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/tablaclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a tabla work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Most drums just go thud. The tabla sings a note you can tune to a song, thanks to a black spot of iron-filing paste that C. V. Raman explained in 1920. Play the dayan and bayan in 3D, watch the drumhead's modes line up, and bend the bass with your palm.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/tablaclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/tablaclear

In this video:
• Two drums, one instrument. The dayan is a hollowed block of sheesham wood played with the right hand; the bayan is a copper or brass bowl for the left.
• A plain drumhead thuds. A stretched round skin rings in patterns called modes, with still nodal lines and circles.
• Raman's black spot. The syahi is many thin layers of paste made with iron filings, soot, rice and gum, heaviest at the centre.
• Where you strike picks the sound. Na strikes the rim while the ring finger rests on the syahi's edge; the round modes are damped and bright harmonics ring.
• The bayan bends. Pressing the heel of the palm into the bayan stretches its skin.
• Tuned to Sa, keeping time. Hammering the gattas down tightens the straps; tapping the gajra fine-tunes by a few cents, until the dayan rings at the song's Sa.
